title: How Trampolines Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain how trampolines work and where they came from. They open with banter about Josh's trampoline park mishap and school gym-class memories, then define a trampoline as a rigid steel frame holding a woven bouncing mat tensioned by coiled springs, and explain that the springs store elastic potential energy that combines with the jumper's kinetic energy to launch them back up. The history covers the trapeze-net inspiration for George Nissen, his early bouncing rig built in his parents' basement, his work with coach Larry Griswold at the University of Iowa using bicycle inner tubes, the steel coils of 1934, the name taken from the Spanish word for springboard, the 1936 founding of the Griswold-Nissen company, the demonstration tours, and the trademark becoming generic. The episode covers trampoline sports (competition, college trampoline, Olympic trampoline since Sydney 2000, and spinoffs like Spaceball, Slam Ball and Bossa Ball), and injury risks, including American Academy of Pediatrics guidance, emergency room statistics, trampoline ankle and the dangers of multiple users. It closes with listener mail correcting an earlier episode's use of pronouns and a note on preferring "enslaved person".

segments.title: Opening banter and trampoline memories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck trade banter, including Josh's trampoline park fall and Chuck's high school trampoline. They discuss gym class trampoline and parachute games, and tease the episode.

segments.title: What a trampoline is and uses
segments.summary: A trampoline is a rigid steel frame with a woven mat held by tight coiled springs. Variations include competition rectangles, home backyard models with nets, and mini trampolines. Competition trampolines have no nets because athletes jump too high.

segments.title: Physics of the trampoline
segments.summary: The trampoline acts as a giant spring. The springs store elastic potential energy, which combines with the jumper's kinetic energy and directs the energy upward toward the center of the mat.

segments.title: Early precursors and trapeze inspiration
segments.summary: Before the trampoline, people bounced on logs, boards and fabric, such as the Lebowski-style parachute toss. Claims of ancient depictions in China, Iran and Egypt could not be verified. George Nissen was inspired as a boy in 1930 by trapeze artists landing on nets.

segments.title: Invention at University of Iowa
segments.summary: Nissen built an early bouncing rig in his parents' basement, then went to the University of Iowa, where he met coach Larry Griswold. They built a nylon mat prototype using bicycle inner tubes, and steel coils were introduced in 1934.

segments.title: Naming the trampoline and the company
segments.summary: Nissen toured with two friends as the Three Leonardos in 1937 and learned the Spanish word for springboard, trampolin, while in Mexico. He adopted it as the name and trademarked it. He and Griswold founded the company in 1936 and sold about ten in the first year. Griswold then sold his share to Nissen.

segments.title: Demonstrations, The Diving Fool and promotion
segments.summary: Because the device was hard to sell without demonstration, Griswold toured with a comedy diving act called The Diving Fool. Nissen then toured to demonstrate trampolines, including a kangaroo photo shoot in Central Park and stunts in Russia and Egypt. Trampolines were promoted for diving, gymnastics, and military and NASA pilot training.

segments.title: Trampoline trademark becoming generic
segments.summary: The trampoline name became generic after Nissen stopped enforcing the trademark in the 1960s. Until then, media had to use terms like rebound tumbling. Trampoline bounce centers have become popular again.

segments.title: Trampoline sports and Olympics
segments.summary: Trampolining is a sport with college competitions not sanctioned by the NCAA. A world championship was held in London at the Royal Albert Hall. Trampoline became an Olympic event in Sydney in 2000. Routines are judged on execution, difficulty and flight time. China and Canada are strong competitors, and Dong Dong is noted as a decorated athlete.

segments.title: Spinoff trampoline sports
segments.summary: Spaceball, Slam Ball and Bossa Ball are trampoline-based games. Spaceball has teams on two trampolines and a tunnel through a net. Slam Ball is a rugby-basketball hybrid with a trampoline dunk area. Bossa Ball combines volleyball and soccer on trampolines and is played in Spain and Brazil.

segments.title: Trampoline injuries and safety
segments.summary: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises against trampolines for children six and under. ER visits and traumatic brain injuries are discussed, along with multi-user dangers and trampoline ankle. Recommendations include netting, padding, no ladders nearby, and one user at a time. Trampoline park deaths and the Think Before You Bounce group are mentioned.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with a plug for the website and email contact and the show's production credits.
